bull_thesis:
The bull case is an expectations gap on a product whose science is already finished. DBV Technologies has one asset that matters: the Viaskin Peanut patch, a skin patch worn at home that gradually desensitises peanut-allergic children. In the Phase 3 VITESSE trial reported on 16 December 2025, 654 children aged four to seven took part across 86 sites; 46.6% of treated children responded at twelve months versus 14.8% on placebo, and the lower edge of the 95% confidence interval on that difference was 24.5 points against a pre-agreed 15-point bar. That is not a borderline result, and safety was clean for a product used on small children.

The regulatory package is in. The US marketing application for a biologic went to the Food and Drug Administration on 29 September 2026 with a request for the faster six-month review clock, the product carries breakthrough designation, the safety package was pre-agreed with the agency in mid-2026, and at the Guggenheim healthcare conference on 9 November 2026 chief executive Daniel Tasse said no outside expert panel is expected. If the faster clock is granted, the approval decision falls around late May 2027.

The commercial case is better than the category's history suggests. The directly comparable product, an approved oral peanut immunotherapy, was discontinued on 31 July 2026 after a $2.6 billion acquisition failed to produce sales - but it failed on repeated clinic up-dosing visits and awkward billing, exactly the friction a home-applied patch removes. Its exit also leaves the desensitisation field empty. DBV is building a 50-to-70-person allergist sales force against roughly 4,500 US allergists, has a distributor and specialty pharmacy in place, bought $4.5 million of pre-launch inventory in the third quarter of 2026, and guides a launch within weeks of a decision.

The price is the argument. At $10.27 on 16 November 2026 the stock is down about 61% from its 52-week high of $26.19 while the programme advanced. Published analyst targets sit at $47 (Citizens JMP, cut from $55 on 29 October 2026) and $46 (Guggenheim, cut from $51 on 30 October 2026), with consensus in the $37 to $45 range; Citizens models roughly $3 billion of peak US sales at a 90% probability of approval, and Cantor Fitzgerald carries unadjusted peak sales of about $1.1 billion for ages four to seven plus about $832 million for ages one to three. A specialist healthcare investor, RA Capital, paid $13.67 per depositary share in cash on 3 August 2026, 33% above today's price, after the manufacturing warning letter was public. Approval on a sober commercial forecast is worth about $22 per depositary share after the launch financing, roughly double the current price.

Conditions the bull case needs: the agency accepts the file in late November 2026 and grants the six-month clock (confirmed in the day-74 letter around mid-December); the contract plant at Fareva Amboise passes its independent mock inspection with all findings closed by 1 February 2027; a launch financing is completed from a position of strength rather than desperation; and the patch achieves even a quarter of the street's peak-sales assumption.
bear_thesis:
The bear case has three legs, and the first one is simply that the event we are being sold is not the event that is scheduled.

First, the timing. Our board recorded an approval decision on 28 November 2026. No such date exists. What falls in late November is the agency's 60-day verdict on whether the application is complete enough to review and which review clock it gets; the formal confirmation usually arrives in the day-74 letter around mid-December 2026. The approval decision is around late May 2027 on the six-month clock and around late September 2027 on the standard ten-month clock, and the agency has not assigned a target date. So the step inside the next 12 days is a high-base-rate procedural one whose good outcome is already assumed in the price - management's own framing on 9 November was that most breakthrough-designated products do get the faster review - while its bad outcome is severe: a ten-month clock pushes the decision past the company's own stated cash runway.

Second, the balance sheet. Cash was $165.7 million at 30 September 2026 against a nine-month net loss of $162.5 million and a third-quarter loss of $64.5 million. The quarterly filing states that substantial doubt exists about the ability to continue as a going concern within twelve months, and guides runway only into the third quarter of 2027. The share count is a third larger than the headline: 314.4 million ordinary shares (62.9 million depositary shares) plus 101.0 million ordinary shares of pre-funded warrants (20.2 million depositary shares, economically already issued), plus 15.0 million options and 10.0 million restricted units - roughly 83 to 88 million depositary shares fully diluted. A $150 million at-the-market share-sale programme was refreshed on 27 July 2026 and is live. Dilution is certain, not contingent, and the only question is the price at which it happens.

Third, manufacturing. Fareva Amboise is DBV's sole commercial patch manufacturer and received an FDA warning letter in April 2026 after a September 2025 inspection of veterinary production at the same site. The findings concerned quality systems and are site-wide in effect, even though they did not involve Viaskin. Remediation is Fareva's responsibility, not DBV's. There is no second site. A clean clinical package plus a failed pre-approval inspection equals a complete response letter and a resubmission - the single most common way a filing like this is lost. DBV itself renegotiated its $1.1 million contribution on 30 September 2026 so that payment turns on Fareva passing an independent mock inspection with no critical findings, no repeat observations and every finding fixed by 1 February 2027: management has priced this risk even as it expresses confidence.

And behind all of it is the category's commercial record. The only approved oral peanut immunotherapy was acquired inside a $2.6 billion deal in August 2020, never sold meaningfully, was divested in September 2023 and discontinued on 31 July 2026. Meanwhile omalizumab, approved on 16 February 2024 to reduce reactions from accidental exposure in food-allergic patients aged one and up, already competes for the same allergist's attention and payer budget with a large brand behind it. The street's $3 billion peak-sales models have no precedent in this category, which is precisely why a stock with a $45 consensus target trades at $10.27.

What confirms the bear case: a refusal to file or a standard ten-month clock in the late-November or mid-December notification; any slippage or adverse finding in the Fareva mock inspection before 1 February 2027; or a large discounted equity raise. On failure the stock is worth cash burned down plus residual technology, about $2.25 to $2.75 per depositary share - roughly 73% to 78% below today's price. Nothing contractual stops that.
sop_bull: Event-win value, about $22 per depositary share, built deliberately below the street rather than on it. Start with the indication actually filed: children aged four to seven, against roughly 2% US childhood peanut-allergy prevalence, and a realistic peak US net sales estimate of $700 million to $800 million by the early 2030s. That is a roughly 30% haircut to Cantor Fitzgerald's unadjusted $1.1 billion for this age band and a small fraction of the $3 billion Citizens models across both bands, because the only comparable product - an approved oral peanut immunotherapy - was discontinued on 31 July 2026 after failing commercially. At a 30% net margin at scale that is about $225 million of annual earnings power at peak. A newly approved, sole-option therapy in an emptied field supports roughly 14 to 16 times those earnings, or $3.2 billion to $3.6 billion, which discounted back from an early-2030s peak at 15% a year is about $1.8 billion to $1.9 billion today. Add an option value of roughly $150 million for the toddler programme (ages one to three; recruitment for the supporting safety study closed in the second quarter of 2026, with a sequential filing agreed with the agency for 2027) and $165.7 million of cash at 30 September 2026, then subtract about $250 million of equity that must still be raised to fund the launch and the burn to breakeven. Equity value lands at roughly $2.0 billion to $2.1 billion over about 95 to 100 million depositary shares post-raise: about $21 to $22 each. Two cross-checks. The street's $37 to $47 is the same arithmetic with a 90% approval probability and $3 billion of peak sales substituted in - that is the upside tail, not the base. And $22 is about 1.6 times the $13.67 a specialist healthcare investor paid in cash on 3 August 2026, a sensible payoff for removing the regulatory risk they were still carrying at that price.
sop_bear: Verified downside floor, about $2.25 to $2.75 per depositary share on outright failure, with an intermediate step at about $5. Derivation. There is no acquirer, no deal consideration, no contractual payout, no announced asset sale and no cash pile that covers the stock - so the board entry's $9.50 floor has no mechanism behind it and should be discarded. What exists is cash: $165.7 million at 30 September 2026, burning roughly $50 million to $55 million a quarter and guided only into the third quarter of 2027, under an explicit statement that substantial doubt exists about the ability to continue as a going concern. On a refusal to file, a complete response letter on manufacturing that cannot be cured, or a wind-down in 2027, cash would be down to roughly $80 million to $100 million, or about $1.00 to $1.20 per diluted depositary share on roughly 83 million shares. Add residual value for the patch platform intellectual property, French research tax-credit receivables and the toddler data set - realistically $100 million to $140 million in a distressed sale or reverse merger, since the technology would just have failed its test - and the floor is about $2.25 to $2.75. The intermediate branch matters more in practice: a fixable manufacturing rejection (findings closed, resubmit, approval roughly a year later) leaves the asset intact but forces a financing from weakness, and that is worth about $5 per depositary share after the dilution it implies. Either way the loss is not bounded by any mechanism; it is bounded only by how fast the cash runs out.
sop_fair_value: About $14 per depositary share, with a working band of $12 to $17
sop_breakdown: Probability-weighted across three outcomes, all per depositary share and all after the financing each path implies. Approval around mid-2027 followed by a credible launch, worth about $22 - probability 55%, contributing $12.10. A manufacturing-driven rejection that is fixable, with a delay and a financing done from weakness before eventual approval, worth about $5 - probability 25%, contributing $1.25. Outright failure or wind-down, worth about $2.50 - probability 20%, contributing $0.50. Total about $13.85, rounded to $14. The 55% first-cycle approval odds sit well below the street's 90% because the clinical package is strong but the sole commercial plant is under an April 2026 FDA warning letter and the agency has not yet inspected it; blending the fixable branch back in puts cumulative eventual-approval odds near 80%, which is a fair read of a trial that cleared its pre-agreed bar by nine percentage points. Components inside the approval branch: the ages four to seven indication at $700 million to $800 million of peak US net sales capitalised and discounted, about $19; the toddler programme option, about $1.50; net cash after the launch raise, about $1.50.
risk_reward: Roughly 1.5 to 1, and the loss is not bounded. From $10.27 on 16 November 2026: upside to the approval-resolved value of $22 is about +114%; upside to the base-case $14 is about +36%; downside to a fixable manufacturing rejection at $5 is about -51%; downside to outright failure at $2.50 is about -76%. Raw asymmetry on target versus floor is therefore about 1.5 to 1 - thin for a single-binary regulatory bet whose deciding event is six to ten months away, and far from the defined-risk profile this funnel is built to buy. The board entry's $9.50 floor against a $9.05 price implied almost no loss on failure; the verified number is about $2.50, so the recorded asymmetry was overstated several-fold. The street's $37 to $47 targets would make this look like 4 to 1; those targets embed a 90% approval probability and $3 billion of peak sales in a category whose only approved competitor was discontinued in July 2026.
catalyst_summary: The decision that re-rates this stock - FDA approval of the Viaskin Peanut patch for children aged four to seven - has no published date and falls around late May 2027 at the earliest, or around late September 2027 without the faster review clock, after a pre-approval inspection of a sole-source contract plant that has been under an FDA warning letter since April 2026. What actually lands inside our 12-day window, around 28 November 2026, is only the agency's verdict on whether the file is complete and which clock it gets, still unannounced as of 16 November 2026. At $10.27 approval is worth about $22 and failure about $2.50 per depositary share: a real expectations gap against a $45 street consensus, but an undated, leveraged bet with a going-concern balance sheet and no floor, not a defined-risk event trade.
dated_milestone: Around 28 November 2026: the 60-day point after the 29 September 2026 submission, by which the FDA decides whether the application is sufficiently complete to permit substantive review and whether it receives the faster six-month clock instead of the standard ten. This is fixed by the filing-review rules rather than by any published company or agency commitment, and the formal notification normally arrives in the agency's day-74 letter around mid-December 2026. Management confirmed the timing at the Guggenheim healthcare conference on 9 November 2026 - the chief executive described late November as the action date on file acceptance - and the 28 October 2026 quarterly release states that the filing-acceptance and priority-review decisions are expected in the fourth quarter of 2026. This is not the approval decision. The second dated gate is 1 February 2027, the contractual deadline by which Fareva Amboise must pass an independent mock pre-approval inspection with no critical findings, no repeat observations and every finding closed, per Amendment No. 1 to the letter of intent signed on 30 September 2026. The approval decision itself remains undated: around late May 2027 on a six-month clock, around late September 2027 on a ten-month clock - the latter past the stated cash runway.
forcing_function:
Three dates, and only the last one re-rates the stock.

Around 28 November 2026, confirmed in writing by about mid-December 2026: file acceptance and the review clock. The faster clock is the expected answer in management's own framing, so the good outcome is worth only a modest move; the standard ten-month clock would push the approval decision to around late September 2027, past the company's stated runway into the third quarter of 2027, and would be punishing. Buying this step means paying for the part of the sequence already in the price.

1 February 2027: the contractual deadline for Fareva Amboise to pass an independent mock pre-approval inspection with all findings closed. This is the real operational test, because the plant has been under an April 2026 FDA warning letter arising from a September 2025 inspection of veterinary production at the same site, and DBV has no alternative manufacturer. A pass largely removes the single biggest reason a strong clinical package fails.

Around late May 2027 (on the six-month clock): the approval decision, and the only event that resolves the thesis. It is six-plus months outside our window and has no published date until the agency assigns one.

A fourth, non-regulatory forcing event sits across all three: the launch financing. With $165.7 million of cash at 30 September 2026, a going-concern warning, and a refreshed $150 million at-the-market programme live since 27 July 2026, a raise is certain. Whether it is priced off strength (after a granted priority clock) or weakness (after a setback) is the main swing factor in what shareholders actually keep.
consensus_delta:
There are two disagreements here pointing in opposite directions, and only one of them is ours.

Where the street is too optimistic, and where we part company with it: Citizens JMP assumes a 90% probability of approval and roughly $3 billion of peak US sales across both age bands; Cantor Fitzgerald carries unadjusted peak sales of about $1.1 billion for ages four to seven plus about $832 million for ages one to three; published targets were $47 (Citizens JMP, 29 October 2026, cut from $55) and $46 (Guggenheim, 30 October 2026, cut from $51), with consensus in the $37 to $45 range. Two of those assumptions are factually hard to defend. The 90% approval probability treats manufacturing as solved, when DBV's sole commercial patch plant has been under an FDA warning letter since April 2026, remediation is a third party's responsibility, there is no second site, and the plant has not yet been inspected for this product. And the $3 billion peak-sales figure has no precedent in this category: the only approved oral peanut immunotherapy was bought inside a $2.6 billion acquisition in August 2020, never sold meaningfully, was divested in September 2023 and was discontinued on 31 July 2026, while omalizumab - approved on 16 February 2024 for reducing reactions from accidental food exposure in patients aged one and up - already competes for the same allergist attention and payer budget.

Where the market is arguably too pessimistic, which is the genuine opportunity: at $10.27 the stock carries about 83 to 88 million fully diluted depositary shares, so roughly $0.9 billion of market value and about $0.7 billion of enterprise value after $165.7 million of cash. That is pricing a trial that cleared its pre-agreed statistical bar by nine percentage points (46.6% versus 14.8% responders, lower confidence bound 24.5 points against a 15-point requirement, 654 children) as closer to a coin flip than the evidence warrants. A specialist healthcare investor paid $13.67 per depositary share on 3 August 2026, after the warning letter was public. The stock is down about 61% from its $26.19 high while the programme advanced. Our view - about $14 of probability-weighted value, $22 on approval - sits between the two camps: more generous than the tape, far more sober than the models.

The third and most specific error is one our own board made, not the street's: recording an approval decision on 28 November 2026. The approval decision has no date. Anyone sizing this as a 12-day dated event is mispricing the calendar by six to eleven months.
valley_of_death:
The next three to nine months are where this position gets hurt even if the science is right.

Cash and the clock. $165.7 million at 30 September 2026 against a third-quarter net loss of $64.5 million (operating expenses $66.3 million, including $47.0 million of research and development with $4.7 million of one-off filing costs) and a nine-month net loss of $162.5 million. Runway is guided only into the third quarter of 2027, and the quarterly filing states that substantial doubt exists about the ability to continue as a going concern within twelve months. Launch spending is already running ahead of approval - $15.7 million of sales and marketing over nine months, $4.5 million of pre-launch inventory in the third quarter, and a 50-to-70-person sales force being hired - so the burn gets worse, not better, before any revenue arrives.

The financing is unavoidable and the overhang is live. A $150 million at-the-market programme was refreshed on 27 July 2026 and was the vehicle for the August placement; 101.0 million ordinary shares of pre-funded warrants (20.2 million depositary shares) already sit on the register. Management's own line on 9 November 2026 was that the number of financing tools available is numerous. Expect equity issuance in the window, and expect it to cap any rally.

The two ways the window itself goes wrong. A refusal to file in late November 2026 would be the worst single outcome and would likely halve the stock. More probable and nearly as damaging: the standard ten-month clock instead of six, which moves the approval decision to around late September 2027 - beyond the stated runway - and forces a larger, cheaper raise. On the other side, a granted six-month clock is the expected outcome and is therefore worth little.

Then manufacturing. Between now and 1 February 2027 Fareva Amboise must pass an independent mock pre-approval inspection with no critical findings and no repeat observations. Any leak of slippage, or an adverse real inspection later in the review, converts a strong filing into a complete response letter and a resubmission roughly a year out - the roughly $5 branch in our valuation, or about 51% below today's price.

Finally, a quieter risk: no outside expert panel is expected, per management on 9 November 2026, but the agency keeps that discretion all the way through. A panel being called would signal doubt where none is currently priced and would reset the timeline again.
positioning_washout:
There is no forced-selling dynamic to harvest here, and that is an important negative finding rather than a neutral one. Short interest is small - roughly 1.4 million depositary shares, between 1.4% and 2.4% of the float, and falling - so there is no crowded bearish position to squeeze on good news. There is no dividend to cut and no income-oriented shareholder base to flush out, because the company has never earned anything. Institutional ownership is reported between roughly 41% and 72% depending on the source, with a specialist healthcare investor adding $50 million at $13.67 per depositary share on 3 August 2026, so the register is already in the hands of people who understand the binary.

The pressure runs the other way. The mechanical supply in this name is issuance, not capitulation: a live $150 million at-the-market programme, 20.2 million depositary shares of pre-funded warrants, and a launch that must be funded. On any strength - a granted six-month clock, a passed mock inspection, an approval - the predictable response is a raise into it. The 61% decline from the $26.19 high since late 2025 looks like ordinary long-horizon de-rating of a cash-hungry single-asset story rather than a forced liquidation, which means the usual argument that the selling is mechanical and therefore price-insensitive does not apply. The holders who are left are informed and voluntary; the stock is cheap because the risk is real, not because somebody has to sell.
moderator_conclusion:
This is a real investment and the wrong trade for this funnel, and the two statements do not conflict.

Start with the correction, because everything follows from it. Our board recorded an FDA approval decision for the Viaskin Peanut patch on 28 November 2026, with a floor of $9.50 against a price of $9.05 - a setup that implied almost no downside. Verified against the primary record as of 16 November 2026, neither half holds. The application went in on 29 September 2026; what falls around 28 November is the agency's 60-day verdict on whether the file is complete and which review clock it gets, normally confirmed in the day-74 letter in mid-December. The approval decision is around late May 2027 on the faster six-month clock, around late September 2027 on the standard clock, and the agency has not assigned a date. And there is no floor at all: no acquirer, no deal terms, no contractual payout. What backstops the price is $165.7 million of cash burning $50 million to $55 million a quarter under an explicit going-concern warning, with runway only into the third quarter of 2027, roughly 83 to 88 million fully diluted depositary shares once 101.0 million ordinary shares of pre-funded warrants are counted, and a live $150 million at-the-market programme. On failure this is worth about $2.50, not $9.50 - the recorded asymmetry was overstated by roughly nine times.

So the catalyst inside our window is a procedural step with the odds pointing the wrong way. The faster clock is the assumed outcome in management's own framing on 9 November 2026, so arriving pays little; a standard ten-month clock pushes the real decision past the cash runway and would hurt badly. That is a small-heads, large-tails coin, and paying up for it is paying for the part of the sequence already in the price. By this committee's definitions the load-bearing event is a third-party, single-binary, undated regulatory decision - real, but not the dated binding trigger the board entry claims - and the aggressive-entry treatment reserved for a firmly dated, floor-backed special situation simply does not apply. The loss here is not defined.

Now the other side, honestly stated. The science is strong: 46.6% of treated children responded versus 14.8% on placebo in 654 children aged four to seven, with the lower edge of the confidence interval at 24.5 points against a pre-agreed 15-point bar. Breakthrough designation, a pre-agreed safety package and no expected expert panel are all in hand. The competing oral immunotherapy was discontinued on 31 July 2026, leaving the desensitisation field empty of a direct rival, and the patch removes exactly the clinic-visit friction that killed it. A specialist healthcare investor paid $13.67 in cash on 3 August 2026, 33% above today's price, with the warning letter already public. Against a probability-weighted value near $14 and an approval outcome near $22, a $10.27 price is cheap - and the street at $37 to $47 shows how violently the market disbelieves the models rather than that the models are right.

The timing call is therefore wait, not pass. The thesis is intact and the gap is genuine; the entry is six weeks early. The specific developments to wait for, in order: the day-74 letter around mid-December 2026 confirming the six-month clock and a first-half-2027 decision date - without that, the whole calendar is wrong; then the Fareva Amboise mock pre-approval inspection passing with no critical findings and no repeat observations by its contractual 1 February 2027 deadline, which is the single most likely way a clean filing still fails; and ideally the launch financing completed, so that the inevitable issuance is behind the position rather than in front of it. Any of those three resolving favourably would justify a venture-scale entry; a price under $8 with the clock already granted would be better again. A refusal to file, a ten-month clock, or a manufacturing setback takes this to the $5 branch or below, and nothing stops it.

On the value question, judged purely against the verified downside: there is effectively no margin of safety. Cash net of near-term burn is about $1.00 to $1.20 per diluted depositary share against an $10.27 price, the going-concern language is in the filings, dilution is certain, and the asset is a single unapproved product manufactured at one plant under an FDA warning letter. There is no franchise and no moat to credit - no product revenue, negative returns on capital, protection limited to patent and regulatory exclusivity on one device-drug combination. That earns the lowest value score on the scale, which is exactly as it should be: this name is owned for the event, or not at all.

## 2. IS THE CATALYST REAL, DATED, AND BINDING?

Three separate events have been collapsed into one on our board. They need separating, because
only the third one pays.

**Event one — completeness and clock decision, around 28 November 2026 (12 days out).** This is
real and it is date-bound by statute: the agency has 60 days from submission to decide whether
the file is complete enough to review substantively, and the same window carries the priority-review
answer. The formal confirmation normally arrives in the agency's day-74 letter, so mid-December
2026. Binding on the agency, yes. But two things gut it as a trade. First, the expected outcome
is already the assumed outcome: outright refusals to file are uncommon, and Tassé's own framing
on the call was that "a large percentage of companies with breakthrough designation do get the
priority review." You are paid little for the base case arriving. Second, the adverse branch is
brutal and asymmetric — a standard ten-month clock pushes the decision to roughly late September
2027, which is *past* the company's stated runway and forces a financing into a weakened tape.
So the dated event inside our window is a coin that pays small heads and large tails. That is
the opposite of the setup this funnel exists to buy.

**Event two — manufacturing, by 1 February 2027.** Fareva Amboise must pass an independent mock
pre-approval inspection with every finding closed. This is the single most load-bearing
operational date and it is contractual, which is unusual and useful. Management's line is
confidence, not evidence: "our confidence this will be resolved prior to our pre-approval
inspection is also very high," and on the quarterly call they were "quite comfortable with
progress." Fareva, not DBV, owns the remediation and files the monthly updates to the agency.
DBV has one manufacturer for this product and no second site. A site-wide warning letter at a
sole-source commercial plant is the classic way a clean clinical package turns into a complete
response letter.

**Event three — the approval decision, undated.** There is no published target action date,
because the agency has not assigned one. Derived from the filing rules, it is around late May
2027 on the six-month priority clock and around late September 2027 on the ten-month standard
clock. This is the event our board priced. It is six to eleven months away, not 12 days, and
until the day-74 letter nobody — including management — can name the day.

**Sponsor credibility on hitting dates.** Mixed, and the mix matters. DBV has been refused a
filing before (2020) and has a history of regulatory timeline slippage; the current team under
Tassé has, in contrast, done what it said through this cycle — it pre-agreed the safety package
with the agency in mid-2026, filed inside the guided window, and raised money before it was
desperate. The toddler programme (ages 1-3) was handled sensibly: recruitment for the supporting
study closed in the second quarter of 2026 and the company deliberately agreed a *sequential*
rather than parallel filing with the agency in 2027 to avoid clogging its own review. That is
the behaviour of a team managing a review, not spinning one.

## 3. THE DOWNSIDE FLOOR — what actually backstops the price

This is where our board entry is not merely optimistic but inverted. It records a floor of
$9.50 against a price of $9.05, implying you cannot lose. Nothing of the kind exists.

There is no acquirer, no deal consideration, no contractual payout, no asset sale and no cash
pile that covers the stock. What there is:

- **Cash $165.7 million** at 30 September 2026, against a nine-month net loss of $162.5 million
  and a third-quarter loss of $64.5 million (operating expenses $66.3 million, of which research
  and development $47.0 million including $4.7 million of one-off filing costs). Runway is
  guided only "into the third quarter of 2027."
- **An explicit going-concern warning**: "substantial doubt exists about the Company's ability
  to continue as a going concern within twelve months."
- **A share count that is bigger than it looks.** 314.4 million ordinary shares (62.9 million
  depositary shares) plus 101.0 million ordinary shares of pre-funded warrants (20.2 million
  depositary shares, economically already issued), plus 15.0 million options and 10.0 million
  restricted units. Call it roughly 83 to 88 million depositary shares fully diluted — about
  a third more than the headline count. Cash is therefore about $2.00 per diluted depositary
  share today, and falling by roughly $0.55 per quarter.
- **A live dilution channel**: a refreshed $150 million at-the-market programme, under which the
  August placement was executed. Management's own words at the conference: "the number of tools
  we have for financing the company are numerous." A commercial launch needs a raise regardless
  of outcome.

So the honest floor ladder, not the board's:

| Outcome | Value per depositary share | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| Fixable manufacturing rejection — approval delayed, resubmission needed, financing done from weakness | about $5 | Residual probability-weighted approval value minus heavy dilution |
| Outright failure or wind-down in 2027 | about $2.25 to $2.75 | Cash burned down to roughly $80-100 million (about $1.00-1.20 per diluted share) plus residual patch technology, French tax-credit receivables, and the toddler data set, in a liquidation or reverse-merger |

Downside from $10.27 is therefore roughly 51% on a fixable setback and roughly 73-78% on
failure. The loss is **not** defined. Calling this a defined-risk special situation would be
a category error.

## 4. CLAIMS vs EVIDENCE (forensic)

| Management claim | Evidence | Read |
|---|---|---|
| "We have asked for priority review. We have breakthrough designation." (9 Nov 2026) | Breakthrough designation is a matter of record; the priority request is in the filing | True, but a request is not a grant, and the grant is decided by a separate agency team |
| No outside expert panel expected ("we're not expecting one") | Pre-filing minutes, per management; the agency keeps discretion throughout | Credible and consistent with a clean, pre-agreed statistical package — but unverifiable by us |
| Warning-letter findings are "unrelated to Viaskin itself" | Correct on origin: the September 2025 inspection concerned a veterinary product | Accurate yet incomplete — the letter's effect is site-wide, and that site is the sole commercial source |
| Launch "weeks from" the decision; 50 to 70 specialty representatives for roughly 4,500 US allergists; distributor and specialty pharmacy in place; $4.5 million of pre-launch inventory bought in the third quarter | Spending is visible in the accounts: sales and marketing $15.7 million over nine months | The build is real and the money is being spent ahead of an unapproved product — commitment, and also burn |
| Runway "into the third quarter of 2027" | $165.7 million against a $54 million average quarterly net loss, rising with launch costs | Arithmetically tight, and it assumes the launch spend does not accelerate before approval |

**The commercial claim nobody on the bull side likes discussing.** The directly comparable
product, an approved oral peanut immunotherapy, was bought by Nestlé inside a $2.6 billion
acquisition in August 2020, never sold meaningfully, was divested to Stallergenes Greer in
September 2023 after a strategic review, and was **discontinued on 31 July 2026**. That is the
base rate for monetising peanut desensitisation in the United States, and it is close to zero.
Two offsets are fair: the patch removes the clinic up-dosing visits and billing friction that
sank the oral product, and the field is now empty of a direct desensitisation competitor. One
further competitor is real and already approved — omalizumab (Xolair) was cleared on 16 February
2024 to reduce reactions from accidental exposure in food-allergic patients aged one and up. It
does different work (protection, not desensitisation) but it competes for the same allergist's
attention and the same payer budget, with an established brand behind it.

Street models do not reflect that base rate. Citizens JMP assumes a 90% probability of approval
in both age groups and roughly $3 billion of peak US sales; Cantor Fitzgerald carries unadjusted
peak sales of about $1.1 billion for ages 4-7 plus about $832 million for ages 1-3. Published
targets were $47 (Citizens JMP, cut from $55 on 29 October) and $46 (Guggenheim, cut from $51
on 30 October), with consensus in the $37 to $45 range. A stock at $10.27 against a $45
consensus is not a market that disagrees politely; it is a market that does not believe the
models.

## 6. RED FLAGS AND GREEN FLAGS

**Red flags**

- Going-concern doubt stated in the third-quarter filing (28 October 2026), with runway only
  "into the third quarter of 2027" — and a standard review clock would put the decision *after*
  that.
- Sole commercial manufacturer under an April 2026 site-wide warning letter; remediation is a
  third party's job; DBV has no alternative site.
- Dilution is certain, not contingent: 101.0 million pre-funded warrant shares already
  overhanging, a refreshed $150 million at-the-market programme, and a launch that must be funded.
- The board's recorded floor ($9.50) is unsupported by any mechanism. The real bust case is
  roughly $2.25 to $2.75.
- The board's recorded catalyst date (28 November 2026, framed as the approval decision) is the
  wrong event. The approval decision is undated.
- Prior refusal-to-file history at this company (2020) on this same programme family.
- The comparable product's commercial record: discontinued July 2026 after a $2.6 billion
  acquisition failed to produce sales.

**Green flags**

- The clinical bar was cleared with room: 46.6% versus 14.8%, lower confidence bound 24.5 points
  against a 15-point requirement, in 654 children. This is not a borderline trial.
- Breakthrough designation, a pre-agreed safety package, and no outside expert panel expected.
- A specialist healthcare investor paid $13.67 per depositary share in cash on 3 August 2026 —
  33% above today's price — having seen the warning letter.
- The manufacturing milestone was made contractual (1 February 2027, no critical findings, no
  repeats), which converts a vague worry into a checkable date.
- Price has fallen about 61% from the 52-week high while the programme advanced, so the
  expectations gap is wide rather than saturated.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The most telling disclosure is the renegotiated Fareva payment: DBV moved its own $1.1 million
from "payable on approval" to "payable on passing an independent mock inspection." A company
confident in its plant does not need to buy that behaviour; a company that has read an April
warning letter does. Read it as management correctly identifying its own biggest risk and
putting a date on it — useful information, and a warning at the same time.

Second signal: the two analyst target cuts on 29 and 30 October, immediately after the
going-concern disclosure, with ratings maintained. The street is trimming for dilution, not for
science.

Third: short interest is small (roughly 1.4 million depositary shares, 1.4% to 2.4% of the
float). There is no crowded bearish position to squeeze, and no forced-selling dynamic in the
holder base. The weakness is organic — a long-horizon, cash-hungry story in a market that will
not pay in advance.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT

**Trajectory: STABLE.** The science strengthened and the balance sheet weakened by roughly equal
amounts over 2026.

**The single thing the director must weigh before sizing this:** the event we thought we were
buying is not in the window, and the floor we thought bounded the loss does not exist. Inside
the next 12 days all that arrives is the agency's verdict on whether the file is complete and
which clock it gets — a high-base-rate step whose good outcome is already assumed and whose bad
outcome (a ten-month clock) pushes the real decision past the cash runway. The decision that
re-rates the stock is around late May 2027 at the earliest and has no published date. Between
here and there sit a contractual manufacturing test on 1 February 2027 at a sole-source plant
under an FDA warning letter, and a financing that must happen regardless of outcome.

That makes this a leveraged, undated, single-binary regulatory bet with an unbounded downside —
not a defined-risk event trade. It can still be a good *investment* at $10.27 against a
probability-weighted value nearer $14 and an approval outcome worth roughly $22; the
expectations gap is genuine and the trial result is strong. But it must be sized as a venture
position, and the honest entry trigger is the day-74 letter in mid-December 2026 confirming a
six-month clock and a first-half-2027 decision date, ideally alongside a closed launch financing
or a passed mock inspection. Buying the procedural step is paying for the part of the sequence
that is already in the price.

**Moat and secular read (largely not applicable).** There is no economic moat to assess: the
company has no product revenue, negative returns on capital, and its protection is patent and
regulatory exclusivity on a single device-drug combination rather than any durable franchise.
No secular force threatens a terminal value that does not yet exist; the structural risk here
is the category's own commercial history, which is a base-rate problem rather than a secular
decline.
